newsitem.title: USA: U.S. trade group warns against tariffs on paper.
newsitem.headline: U.S. trade group warns against tariffs on paper.

text.p: The president of the American Forest & Paper Association on Tuesday said the elimination of international trade barriers was crucial to the U.S. paper industry, and he identified Finland as an obstacle to achieving that goal.
"We simply can't compete with one hand tied behind our back," said W. Henson Moore, the association's president and chief executive, referring to international tariffs that impede U.S. exports.
Moore was speaking at a media conference during Paper Week, the industry's annual convention in New York.
Moore said countries outside Europe, such as Indonesia, were establishing a world-class paper industry, and that many of these countries had very low production costs.
"How are we are going to compete with them if they have tariffs to boot?" he said.

The U.S. and Canadian paper industries have pushed for an accelerated timetable on eliminating tariffs, setting a goal of January 1998, instead the year 2004 as agreed during the Uruguay Round of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade in 1994.
At a World Trade Organization meeting in Singapore at the end of 1996, the North American paper industry lost its case for speeding up the tariff reduction.

To be sure, there are other European countries with tariffs, but the association believes some of them are willing to eliminate them at an earlier date. Finland is one of those countries blocking progress, Moore said.
"That is something I will be taking up with the Finnish ambassador to the U.S. in very short order," he said.
Moore said the U.S. paper industry could not afford to waste much more time. He said if a European country was willing to address the tariff issue, it could be dealt with on a unilateral basis.
The association president also said the industry would probably have to be more strident in pressing for its demands in negotiations with the United States government.
Finnish tariffs reached a high of more than seven percent on certain paper products, said Maureen Smith, vice president, international of the American Forest & Paper Association.
She said the U.S. paper industry was concerned because the industry saw exports as its best source of growth.
The association has conducted studies showing U.S. exports to Western Europe could increase by $1.0 to $1.5 billion a year if tariffs were leveled, she said.
